summary:
Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or trans identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, inserted by religious legislators into a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape and signed into law in July 1992, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner"; the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality challenge in March 1994. The provision's vagueness had also made it usable against LGBT-rights organising and sexual-health work. Its language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since.

Formal legality does not translate into protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Nicaragua documents a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived opponents of the government that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among the year's significant human rights violations. The official US assessment places anti-LGBTI abuse inside a broader climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International's May 2019 reporting places homophobia inside that same repression. The crackdown on protests that began in April 2018 left at least 325 people dead and more than 2,000 injured, according to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, and journalist Miguel Mora described being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay.

Documented violence against LGBT people is persistent and under-recorded. A 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey counted 53 aggressions between 1999 and 2011, among them 15 murders: 10 gay men, 4 transgender people and 1 lesbian, with the true total expected to be higher. The NGO Programa Feminista La Corriente reported 67 assaults, 1 hate crime or murder and 2 suicides in 2021; 39 assaults, 3 hate crimes and 1 suicide in 2022; 35 assaults, 2 hate crimes, 1 murder, 1 suicide, 2 sexual assaults and 1 extortion in 2023; and 13 assaults, 5 hate crimes and 1 missing person in the first two quarters of 2024. Trans women are the most targeted group, and state police are among the aggressors, tied with family members in 2022. Attacks go largely unreported out of fear of retaliation and poor legal outcomes.

Family-law exclusion is explicit. The Family Code approved by the Nicaraguan Congress in June 2014, in force from 8 April 2015, limits marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples, and Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on voluntary agreement between a man and a woman. Same-sex couples and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. Several organisations filed an action of unconstitutionality against the Code. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that parties to the American Convention on Human Rights must grant same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration rights including marriage, and no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.

Discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is barred in several settings, including health care. Ministerial Resolution 671-2014 bars discrimination in access to health services on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, which is the provision most directly relevant to a visitor seeking care.

Public opinion is largely opposed. A Pew survey conducted from 9 November to 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed to same-sex marriage, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, while the 2017 AmericasBarometer showed 24.5% support.
tangentialFactors:
Media reporting is largely suppressed, much of the media having been restricted since the 2018 protests, which limits coverage of LGBT issues and reduces the visibility of both incidents and legal developments to anyone outside the country.

Public visibility is uneven. Gay men are generally more visible in public than lesbians, who often socialise privately, and an annual Gay Pride celebration has been held in the capital around 28 June since the country's first public pride festival in 1991. Pride events and private socialising carry different exposure profiles in a climate where attacks are tolerated and police appear among aggressors.

The Amnesty International account of the post-2018 crackdown supplies a comparison point: political repression and anti-LGBT hostility are not separate tracks, and a journalist beaten by a pro-government mob was targeted partly for being gay.
localsOnly:
Article 315 of the Penal Code, covering offences against labour rights, punishes discrimination based on "sexual option" by up to one year in prison in employment. Article 3(l) of Law No. 820 prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation grounds in the HIV and AIDS context, and Article 36(5) of the Penal Code makes sexual-orientation discrimination an aggravating circumstance when any criminal offence is committed.

Residents in same-sex relationships have no access to marriage, joint partnership registration or adoption, and households headed by same-sex couples are excluded from the legal benefits attached to opposite-sex marriage under the 2015 Family Code and Article 72 of the Constitution. The action of unconstitutionality filed against the Code is the domestic route being pursued by the organisations concerned.

Documented incidents are compiled by civil-society groups rather than official bodies: Programa Feminista La Corriente issues the recurring counts, and the 2012 Center for Justice and International Law survey remains the long-run baseline. Reporting of attacks is suppressed by fear of retaliation and by poor expected legal outcomes.
outOfScopeNotes:
One source in the inventory, the Franklin & Marshall Global Barometers country page for Nicaragua, records no documented finding for this jurisdiction; nothing in this record is drawn from it.

The outcome of the action of unconstitutionality filed against the 2015 Family Code is unresolved in the sources, as is any Nicaraguan implementation of the 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion.

No youth-specific care-access findings are recorded, and entry, visa and document or gender-marker rules for trans visitors are not sourced in this inventory.
